title: VLT, Keck, and Gemini characterization of the temporarily captured flyby 2026 QQ$_8$
byline: Bolin; Bryce T; Alcorn; Leo Y; Tholen; David J; Lemaux; Brian C; Kim; Eunchong; Alamos; Leila; Berghuis; Jennie L; Boffin; Henri M J; Häußler; Boris; Kasikov; A
html:
Abstract:Very Large Telescope, Keck I, and Gemini North photometry of 2026 QQ$_8$ on November 7-21 gives Sloan Digital Sky Survey-equivalent colors $g-r=0.594^{+0.056}_{-0.053}$, $g-i=0.840^{+0.066}_{-0.065}$, and $i-z=-0.104^{+0.067}_{-0.057}$ mag. Apollo 17 basalt slabs 75075,197 and 71055,239 fit the colors (reduced $\chi^2$ of 0.57 and 0.89). The Bus-DeMeo Sq- and K-type templates give reduced $\chi^2=0.87$ and 0.90, respectively. The colors permit both an Sq-like asteroid and exposed lunar basalt. With revised Keck timing uncertainties, 71 positions (August 19-November 21) give an outward acceleration of $(1.363\pm0.090)\times10^{-10}$ au day$^{-2}$ at 1 au, implying an area-to-mass ratio of $(6.02\pm0.40)\times10^{-4}$ m$^2$ kg$^{-1}$ for a unit radiation-pressure coefficient. For pre-encounter analogues, NEOMOD3 assigns source probabilities of 78.8% to the $\nu_6$ resonance and 20.6% to Jupiter's 3:1 resonance. For a sphere with $H=31.37\pm0.34$, the diameter, density, and mass are ($1.44^{+0.28}_{-0.23}$ m, $1.73^{+0.36}_{-0.30}$ g cm$^{-3}$, $2.73^{+1.19}_{-0.82}\times10^3$ kg) for the Sq albedo ($p_V=0.243\pm0.039$), ($1.62^{+0.28}_{-0.24}$ m, $1.54^{+0.29}_{-0.24}$ g cm$^{-3}$, $3.43^{+1.30}_{-0.94}\times10^3$ kg) for NEOMOD3 ($p_V=0.191$), and ($2.49^{+0.42}_{-0.36}$ m, $1.00^{+0.19}_{-0.16}$ g cm$^{-3}$, $8.09^{+3.06}_{-2.22}\times10^3$ kg) for lunar slabs ($p_V=0.081$). With radiation pressure, nominal capture lasts 224.96 days (April 26-December 7). Sun-Earth corotating geocentric longitude advances 0.76 turns, classifying 2026 QQ$_8$ as a temporarily captured flyby. Its three-dimensional corotating path tangent turns 1.33 revolutions. After 10,000 yr, about 800 of 1,000 clones survive in each model, with about 200 colliding with Earth. The paired survival difference (radiation pressure plus gravity minus gravity only) is ~2 percentage points.
